title: Cooperation
author: Nick Hart
summary: In the fifth post of his series on Richard Claydon's six sense-making disciplines, Nick Hart presents cooperation as the discipline that moves work across teams, roles and time, so that well-framed ideas do not stall in implementation. He identifies its breakdowns in schools as duplicated effort, unclear handovers, initiatives that lose momentum and teams working hard but not together. His central claim is that alignment cannot rely on goodwill and must rest on shared structures, which he develops through four strategies: DARE grids for role clarity, shared artefacts and documents, a planned rhythm of the year, and calendar discipline. Each is justified by the coordination failure it prevents, such as ownership dispersing when roles are implicit or urgency dominating without a predictable cycle. He concludes that these are coordination habits rather than bureaucratic controls, and that thinking well together only matters when teams also coordinate well together.
points: Hart argues that cooperation depends on shared structures rather than goodwill, and that it should strengthen coordination without increasing control.
DARE grids clarify who decides, advises, recommends and executes before work begins, preventing duplicated effort and dispersed ownership.
Shared documents and trackers move coordination out of conversation and memory, so continuity rests on systems rather than individuals.
A mapped rhythm of the academic year and an audited calendar let teams anticipate rather than react, with the calendar treated as a strategic coordination tool.
The strategies are aimed at situations where teams agree on direction yet progress stays slow because they work in parallel rather than in concert.
quotes: Cooperation shapes how work moves across teams, roles and time. Without it, even well framed and well discussed ideas stall in implementation.

In complex organisations, alignment cannot rely on goodwill alone; it depends on shared structures. The cooperation discipline contains core strategies that strengthen coordination without increasing control.
Explicit role clarity prevents duplication and protects pace. When roles remain implicit, decisions blur and ownership disperses. The DARE grid stabilises responsibility before work begins.

These artefacts become reference points that reduce dependence on memory and informal networks. When documentation is fragmented, coordination relies on individuals rather than systems. Shared artefacts create continuity.
A shared rhythm allows teams to anticipate rather than react. Without rhythm, urgency dominates. Work clusters unpredictably.
The calendar becomes an instrument of coordination rather than a record of busyness. When calendars are unmanaged, cooperation fragments.
Teams may agree on direction and even think well together, yet progress remains uneven. Cooperation enables alignment to move from intention to implementation.
